2009-02-19: CDC researchers report that 98.5 percent of tested U.S. influenza A (H1N1) viruses were resistant to oseltamivir (Tamiflu), with four resistant-strain patients having died.
2009-04-21: U.S. health officials report that a new type of swine flu has infected at least two children in California, both of whom recovered, and say they are looking for more cases.
2009-04-25: The World Health Organization warned that a new swine flu strain that killed up to 68 people in Mexico could start a global epidemic, as tests showed the virus might be spreading in the United States.
2009-04-26: The UK health secretary says Tamiflu has proved effective on swine flu patients in Mexico, and testing shows the H1N1 virus can be treated with antivirals Tamiflu and Relenza.
The current swine flu outbreak is of the same strain, H1N1, as the great flu pandemic of 1918.
The U.N. World Health Organization and U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention are collecting samples of the new H1N1 swine flu virus to make a vaccine in case it is needed.
The World Health Organisation warns that the H1N1 swine flu outbreak has "pandemic potential" as more than 80 people have died in Mexico and cases are reported in the US and New Zealand.
2009-04-27: Replikins Ltd. states that its Replikin Count genomics technology provided advance warning of the Mexican H1N1 swine flu outbreak and that a synthetic H1N1 Replikins vaccine is available for testing.
British scientists at the National Institute for Biological Standards and Control began work on a vaccine against the H1N1 swine flu virus.
Fears of a global flu pandemic grew as a dangerous new strain of swine flu (H1N1) killed up to 81 people in Mexico and spread to the United States, Canada, and other countries.

The World Health Organization revised its six-point pandemic alert scale, specifying that phase 5 would signal a pandemic is imminent, as an emergency committee assessed a swine flu outbreak that had killed up to 149 people in Mexico and spread worldwide.
The swine flu crisis lays bare the meat industry's monstrous power, with the Mexico swine flu outbreak alerting the world to a highly globalised industry with global political clout.
A Chinese virologist warns that a possible swine flu pandemic could not be contained within a short time and that China and India would be ill-prepared to handle it.
Live samples of swine flu are to arrive imminently in UK labs, where scientists at the National Institute for Medical Research plan to analyze them to combat the disease.

An outbreak of a new H1N1 influenza strain, apparently related to the 1918-19 pandemic and containing swine, avian and human genetic material, has infected more than 1,000 people in Mexico with over 80 deaths and spread to several areas within the United States and to New Zealand.
The WHO raised its pandemic alert level for the swine flu virus to phase 4, indicating a significantly increased risk of a pandemic.
2009-04-28: The first cases of swine flu are confirmed in Europe, with two people in Scotland and one man in Spain testing positive, as the WHO raises its alert level from three to four.

Stricter swine flu tests cut Mexico's confirmed H1N1 death toll from 20 to seven, while officials warn the number of deaths likely caused by swine flu has risen to 159 with more than 1,300 patients under observation.
Manufacturers take first preparatory steps to develop a vaccine against a new H1N1 swine flu strain that has killed up to 149 people in Mexico and threatens to become a pandemic.
U.S. officials argue for changing the name from swine flu to H1N1 virus because the name is hurting U.S. pork producers' business.

The World Health Organisation calls the H1N1 swine flu virus, which has infected an estimated 1,000 people and killed around 150 in Mexico, an "international public health emergency" that could reach global pandemic levels.

China's cabinet, led by Premier Wen Jiabao, formulated an 8-point flu prevention strategy including strengthened inspection for swine flu outbreaks among pigs and supervision of live pig trade, while China banned pork imports from Mexico and three US states.
2009-04-29: Vials containing samples of the swine flu virus are being sent from the US to a government laboratory north of London as the race for a vaccine begins, with tests underway to determine whether the current seasonal flu vaccine could provide cross protection against the new H1N1 swine flu.
The European Union's executive Commission avoids using "swine flu" to refer to the H1N1 virus, preferring "novel flu," in order to calm consumers and protect the pork industry.
Egypt begins a mass slaughter of thousands of pigs in an effort to prevent swine flu spreading, despite there being no cases of swine flu in Egypt.

The new H1N1 swine flu has spread to nine countries, may have infected more than 2,500 people and killed dozens in Mexico, including a toddler from Mexico visiting Texas who became the first U.S. death.
The World Health Organization raised its swine flu alert level to phase 5, the last step before a pandemic, as the H1N1 virus spread and killed a toddler in Texas, the first death outside Mexico.
2009-04-30: Novartis AG said it will use data from a study on its pre-pandemic bird flu vaccine Aflunov and adjuvant MF59 to help develop a vaccine against the H1N1 swine flu virus.
No cases of H1N1 swine flu had been reported in Africa, though cases had been confirmed almost everywhere else.
The CDC states that no vaccine exists to protect humans from swine flu, although it is formulating one, and that people cannot catch swine flu from eating pork.
Twelve countries have confirmed cases of the H1N1 strain, a new infection that has brought the world to the brink of a pandemic.

Egypt began seizing and slaughtering herds of pigs as a precaution against H1N1 swine flu, despite farmer resistance and UN criticism that the mass cull was a mistake because the virus has not been found in pigs.
U.S. officials said the national total of confirmed H1N1 swine flu cases had risen to 109, with only one fatality recorded in the country.

Mexico began shutting down parts of its economy to slow the spread of a new H1N1 flu strain, as the WHO maintained its alert level one step below full pandemic and stopped referring to the virus as "swine flu."
2009-05-01: Mexico City begins a five-day nationwide shutdown to halt the spread of the H1N1 flu virus, as authorities say the epidemic appears to be easing.

Samples of the H1N1 virus arrived at the National Institute for Medical Research in north London, where scientists will grow the virus structure and study how it might evolve to help develop a vaccine.

US health experts report that the H1N1 swine flu outbreak in Mexico may not be as severe as it first appeared, with many mild cases not immediately noticed, though the WHO fears it could tip into a pandemic.
2009-05-02: The World Health Organisation confirms 787 H1N1 infections in 17 countries.
Mexico's H1N1 swine flu outbreak appeared to be stabilizing, though officials warned the virus still threatened a global pandemic and the WHO said a pandemic was imminent.
2009-05-03: Mexico announced that its H1N1 swine flu epidemic had passed the worst, while experts said the new virus might be no more severe than normal flu.

The head of the World Health Organisation, Margaret Chan, suggested the swine flu pandemic alert would eventually move to its highest level, while officials insisted there were no imminent plans to raise the alert level.
2009-05-04: Pharmacists in the United Arab Emirates ignored regulations on Tamiflu sales to meet "panic" demand following the H1N1 flu outbreak.
Another nine UK cases of swine flu are confirmed, bringing the total to 27, with five being year seven pupils from Alleyn's School in Dulwich, south London, marking the fourth school to close.
2009-05-05: A Texas woman in her 30s with underlying health problems dies from the new H1N1 swine flu, marking the second death outside Mexico.
Five schools in England are closed after pupils fell ill with the H1N1 swine flu virus, with GCSE and A-level exams rescheduled.
The US government says the swine flu virus may be less severe than feared, as the UK confirms one more case and the WHO begins distributing 2.4 million antiviral treatments to 72 countries.

With Mexico saying the worst may be over and the new H1N1 virus starting to look more like a seasonal flu strain in the United States and elsewhere, critics are going to start asking if public health officials overreacted to the outbreak.
2009-05-06: The World Health Organization cautions that meat from pigs infected with the new H1N1 virus should not be used for human consumption and says it is drawing up guidelines to protect workers handling pigs.
A pig at Kabul Zoo, believed to be Afghanistan's only pig, is placed in quarantine over fears it could spread the H1N1 swine flu virus.
2009-05-07: The new H1N1 strain of flu, commonly called swine flu, has not reached the pandemic proportions originally feared, though it has sparked global jokes, disinformation, and various responses such as quarantining a pig in Afghanistan and culling pigs in Egypt.
Four children and one adult linked to Alleyn's School in Dulwich, south-east London, are diagnosed with swine flu, taking the total number of UK cases to 39.
Two new cases of swine flu are diagnosed in the UK, one in a child at a school already closed due to the outbreak, bringing the UK total to 34.
2009-05-08: British scientists announced they had worked out the full genetic code for the swine flu virus, a step expected to aid vaccine development, as the WHO raised its global tally of confirmed H1N1 cases to more than 2,300 and the UK confirmed five new cases.

The UK chief medical officer warns that swine flu may be more infectious than currently appears and that guidance on catching it may have to be changed, while the WHO says unchecked H1N1 could affect almost a third of the population.
2009-05-09: Japan and Australia announce their first cases of the new H1N1 flu.
A Washington state man with underlying heart conditions died from H1N1 influenza, becoming the third U.S. death from the virus.
2009-05-10: The U.S. CDC reports 2,532 confirmed H1N1 swine flu cases in 44 states and three deaths.
The WHO reports that H1N1 flu has infected 4,379 people in 29 countries, with Mexico reporting 1,626 confirmed cases and 45 deaths, and Costa Rica reporting its first death.
The US has more confirmed swine flu cases than any other country, with 2,254 confirmed cases and a third death reported.
2009-05-11: A top WHO official says the H1N1 virus has not shown signs of sustained person-to-person spread outside North America and has not yet tipped over into a pandemic, as WHO laboratories confirm 4,379 infections with the new strain.

Researchers report that the new H1N1 flu strain acts more like a pandemic strain than regular seasonal flu, having killed 56 people in Mexico and likely infected as many as 23,000 Mexicans by late April.
2009-05-12: A World Health Organization expert says most H1N1 flu patients do not require antiviral therapy to recover, but stresses the importance of developing a pandemic vaccine due to the risk of future drug resistance.
The WHO warns that the new H1N1 flu virus could still mutate into a more virulent form and spark an influenza pandemic that could circle the globe up to three times.
Researchers say the H1N1 swine flu virus has "full pandemic potential" and could infect a third of the world's population within six to nine months, though they declined to estimate the death toll.
2009-05-14: A World Health Organization official says the H1N1 flu strain has not yet taken hold outside the Americas but the outbreak is serious and requires close monitoring, with the pandemic alert maintained at Phase 5.
2009-05-16: The World Health Organization is closely monitoring an outbreak of H1N1 swine flu in Japan after three students from the same high school who had not traveled abroad were confirmed infected, while Turkey and India confirmed their first cases.

Health negotiators from rich and poor countries failed to reach a full deal on virus sharing for vaccine production, though they forwarded a framework agreement with gaps to the World Health Assembly, amid the H1N1 outbreak.
2009-05-17: A New York City school principal died from the H1N1 swine flu virus, becoming the city's first death from the illness.
The World Health Organization reports that confirmed H1N1 swine flu cases have risen to 8,480 with 72 deaths, as the virus spreads to 39 countries.
2009-05-18: Japan confirmed 125 people had been infected with the new H1N1 flu strain, as the WHO said humanity may be witnessing an influenza pandemic unfold.
The head of the World Health Organization says the H1N1 flu virus is likely to keep spreading rapidly between people, within countries and across the globe.
Asian health experts and officials express concern that Asia is less prepared for H1N1 vaccine production because more than 90 percent of flu vaccine production capacity is located in the West.

U.S. health officials report that the H1N1 swine flu virus has spread to 48 states, is causing a disproportionate number of hospitalizations among children, teenagers, and young adults, and has killed a New York City school vice principal.
2009-05-19: WHO Director-General Margaret Chan said vaccine makers could produce 4.9 billion pandemic flu shots per year in the best-case scenario, while UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon warned that the world may be in a grace period with H1N1 but is still in the danger zone.
Health officials in Japan confirmed the first cases of swine flu in Tokyo, with two schoolgirls testing positive for the H1N1 virus after returning from a trip to New York.
2009-05-20: The World Health Organization reports that confirmed cases of the new Influenza A (H1N1) flu have risen to 10,243 and the death toll has edged up to 80.
2009-05-21: The Philippines records its first H1N1 case and new infections are confirmed in Japan, China, and Taiwan as the virus spreads in Asia.
2009-05-22: The WHO rethinks its criteria for declaring a global flu pandemic, saying it will look for events signifying a substantial increase in risk of harm to people rather than relying solely on the geographic spread of the H1N1 virus.
WHO chief Margaret Chan warns countries to prepare for more severe H1N1 flu infections and deaths, saying the virus must be closely monitored in Asia, Africa and South America.
2009-05-25: The WHO reports the H1N1 flu strain has spread to Taiwan, Kuwait, Iceland, Switzerland and Honduras, with 12,515 confirmed infections and 91 deaths globally.
2009-05-26: The number of swine flu cases in Australia doubled in the last day to 59, with the virus confirmed in most Australian states and territories.
2009-05-27: The World Organization for Animal Health says more cases of humans transmitting the H1N1 flu strain to pigs are likely but would not be a major concern because swine are not severely affected by the virus.
2009-05-28: Scientists used bird flu virus samples from Egypt to develop a new basis for a vaccine against the H5N1 strain, while the H1N1 swine flu strain continued to spread with over 13,000 infections and 95 deaths, and British scientists produced a strain of H1N1 virus that could be used for large-scale vaccine production.
2009-05-29: Swine flu is spreading more rapidly in Britain than anywhere else in the European Union, with Britain the only member state where more people caught the disease at home than abroad.
2009-06-01: AstraZeneca's MedImmune unit wins an initial $90 million order from the U.S. government to make a live attenuated vaccine against the new H1N1 flu strain.
Cases of the new H1N1 flu virus have been found in all 50 U.S. states and tests have confirmed the virus in more than 10,000 people across the country, with California reporting its first two deaths.
A leading UK flu expert predicts that an H1N1 swine flu pandemic is likely to strike Britain in the autumn as schools and workplaces reopen.
2009-06-02: The number of swine flu (H1N1) cases in the UK climbed to more than 330, with over 60 new cases recorded on Tuesday, while scientists at GSK began analyzing a sample of the virus to develop a vaccine.
2009-06-09: The WHO says it is on the verge of declaring the first influenza pandemic in more than 40 years due to the sustained spread of the H1N1 strain, but wants to ensure countries are prepared to prevent panic.
Concerns are raised that industrial pig farms act as "perfect incubating systems" for novel flu viruses amid the global spread of H1N1 swine flu, which has caused over 120 deaths.
2009-06-10: Drugmakers said they had obtained the new H1N1 flu seed virus and were on track to have a vaccine ready for the northern hemisphere autumn.
The World Health Organization says a sharp increase in swine flu cases in Australia may mean the H1N1 infection has become a pandemic, but no decision has been taken on moving to phase six.
2009-06-11: German authorities confirmed 30 cases of H1N1 flu at a Japanese school in Dusseldorf, the most concentrated outbreak in Germany at that time.
The World Health Organization declared the new H1N1 swine flu a full pandemic, as researchers reported the virus had circulated undetected in pigs for years.
2009-06-12: Novartis AG expects an H1N1 vaccine to be available by autumn after producing the first batch for testing ahead of schedule, while Baxter International said its A/H1N1 vaccine could be ready for commercial use as early as next month.
2009-06-15: The WHO reported laboratory-confirmed cases of H1N1 with a mortality rate of 0.45%, contradicting earlier estimates of 5-6%.
A female patient in Scotland becomes the first person in the UK to die after being confirmed with the H1N1 swine flu virus.
2009-06-17: Venezuela quarantines a Spanish cruise ship after three crew members were diagnosed with the H1N1 flu virus, while Barbados and Grenada refuse to allow its passengers to disembark.
Israeli President Shimon Peres and staff at his official home were cleared of H1N1 virus infection after he was tested for swine flu following a meeting with a group later found to be infected.
China plans to restrict movement in residential areas and shut down entertainment centres under worst-case contingency plans to prevent the H1N1 flu strain from spreading.
Government officials warned that anyone with flu symptoms should stay away from pigs after preliminary experiments showed the H1N1 virus could potentially infect and transmit among pigs.
2009-06-18: South Africa confirms its first swine flu case, a 12-year-old boy who flew in from the US, marking the first known case of the H1N1 virus in sub-Saharan Africa.
2009-06-19: Drug makers are gearing up to make vaccines against the new H1N1 virus, starting test batches and pledging free doses for poor countries, while governments pledge billions for the vaccine as the World Health Organization declared a pandemic.

The new H1N1 flu strain is causing an extended year-round flu season in the United States that disproportionately hits young people, with ongoing transmission possibly continuing into the fall and winter, according to CDC officials.
2009-06-22: The World Health Organization reports a sharp increase in global H1N1 swine flu cases, with 52,160 laboratory-confirmed cases and 231 deaths across around 100 countries and territories.
2009-06-23: Germany's federal agency for infectious diseases says there are signs the H1N1 swine flu virus has started to mutate and warns it could spread in a more aggressive form in the coming months.
Argentine health officials report seven more swine flu deaths, bringing the country's total to 17.
2009-06-26: U.S. health officials estimate that more than 1 million people in the United States may have been infected with the new H1N1 swine flu, with infections continuing to rise.
Experts report the first case of swine flu resistant to Tamiflu, in a patient in Denmark, while the UK announces a jump in confirmed swine flu cases and a third death.
2009-06-29: A report shows the new H1N1 swine flu strain spread along airline routes, with the WHO confirming 70,893 cases and 311 deaths, and Iraq, Lithuania, Monaco and Nepal confirming their first cases.
Scientists establish the first case of the new H1N1 influenza strain showing resistance to Tamiflu, though Danish officials say it poses no threat to public health.
2009-06-30: A case of Tamiflu resistance in an H1N1 swine flu patient in Denmark appears to be drug-induced, with no sign yet of a resistant strain circulating.
